passage: The little grocery shop near the bus stand would shut at eight, and the clock said twenty to. Bidisha's mother had given her a long list in a hurry: apples, bananas, spinach, tomatoes, onions, milk, curd, paneer. Her brother Ojas hopped beside her. "That's so many!" Bidisha stopped outside the door. "Three groups," she said. "Fruits first: apples, bananas. Vegetables: spinach, tomatoes, onions. Then milk, curd, paneer." She repeated it in the queue, and went through the shop one shelf at a time. Nothing was missed, and Ojas carried the bag home, proud to be useful.

qa.q: When would the grocery shop shut?
qa.a: The shop would shut at eight.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling outside the shop, and how did the grouping help?
qa.a: Bidisha felt pressed for time and a little overwhelmed by the long list, but three groups turned one big list into three small ones she could hold.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Bidisha use, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha could ask her mother to write the list down or take a picture of the list to check in the shop. That would keep the items in front of her even when rushed.

qa.q: How does the shopping trip look to Ojas?
qa.a: Ojas hopped along, said there were so many items and later carried the bag proudly, so Ojas felt part of the job and pleased to help.

grounding: A child sorts a long shopping list into fruits, vegetables and dairy before entering the shop, so three small groups replace one long list.

passage: Outside the vegetable market in Lajpat Nagar, Gargi's father, Jeevan, read out the list on his phone: "Apples, milk, onions, bananas, curd, tomatoes, paneer, oranges, potatoes." Gargi held up a hand. "Stop. Nine things jumping around. Let me fix it." She tapped her fingers. "Fruits: apples, bananas, oranges. That's one. Vegetables: onions, tomatoes, potatoes. Two. Milk things: milk, curd, paneer. Three." "And?" "And now it's three little lists of three, not one big list of nine. The fruit man, the vegetable woman, the dairy." Jeevan put his phone away as a test. Gargi led him from stall to stall and they came out with every item, and one packet of peanuts that was not on any list.

qa.q: How many things were on the list Jeevan read out?
qa.a: There were nine things on the list.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel about the long list before she sorted it?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed by nine things "jumping around", and then confident once the groups made sense.

qa.q: What else could help Gargi if the list had twenty items?
qa.a: She could still group them but also jot the groups on paper, because even small groups add up when a list is very long.

qa.q: How does Gargi's plan look to her father?
qa.a: Jeevan is curious and a little impressed, trusting her enough to put his phone away as a test.

grounding: It shows a child sorting a shopping list into fruits, vegetables and milk items so she remembers three small groups instead of one long list.

passage:
"Yogesh, get the shopping, na? My hands are full of dough."
"How much?"
"Rice flour, bananas, carrots, butter, peas, papaya, cheese, lemons, beans, yoghurt. Can you remember that?"
"Wait, Mumma. Say it again slowly."
Tanuja said it again. Yogesh closed his eyes.
"Okay, fruits: bananas, papaya, lemons."
"Lemons are fruits?"
"In my list they are. Vegetables: carrots, peas, beans. Dairy: butter, cheese, yoghurt."
"And rice flour?"
"Rice flour is alone. It's a one-thing group."
Tanuja laughed. "Say it back without looking."
"Three fruits, three vegetables, three dairy, one flour. Ten."
"Off you go then."

qa.q: Which items did Yogesh put in the dairy group?
What does Yogesh asking to hear the list slowly suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt a little worried the list was too long, and wanted time to sort it before trusting himself.

qa.q: What else could Yogesh do at the shop to be sure he has everything?
qa.a: He could count the items in each group as he pays, so a missing one shows up right away.

qa.q: How does Yogesh's grouping look to Tanuja?
qa.a: Tanuja is amused by the "one-thing group" and pleased that he can say it all back, so she trusts him to go.

grounding: It shows a child grouping a shopping list by type so there are a few small lists to remember instead of one long one.
